person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: belief in conspiracy theories, and whether the motives that attract people to them are satisfied by them
span.quote: However, little research has investigated the consequences of conspiracy belief, and to date, this research does not indicate that conspiracy belief fulfills people’s motivations. Instead, for many people, conspiracy belief may be more appealing than satisfying.

span.label: what psychological factors drive conspiracy belief, and what its consequences are for the believer
span.quote: We review the current research and find that it answers the first of these questions more thoroughly than the second.

span.label: a three-motive organising schema - epistemic, existential, social - and the finding that the literature answers the drivers far better than the consequences
span.quote: This research suggests that people may be drawn to conspiracy theories when—compared with nonconspiracy explanations—they promise to satisfy important social psychological motives that can be characterized as epistemic (e.g., the desire for understanding, accuracy, and subjective certainty), existential (e.g., the desire for control and security), and social (e.g., the desire to maintain a positive image of the self or group). This taxonomy, derived from system-justification theory, serves as a useful heuristic to classify the motives associated with conspiracy belief.

span.label: critique
span.quote: We review the current research and find that it answers the first of these questions more thoroughly than the second.

span.label: conspiracy belief as motivated social cognition that may thwart the very motives it answers
span.quote: Nevertheless, preliminary work suggests that despite the allure of conspiracy beliefs for people who have heightened epistemic, existential, and social motives, they may ultimately thwart those motives further. In this sense, conspiracy theories might be seen as an ironic or self-defeating manifestation of motivated social cognition.

span.label: narrative review of the current experimental and correlational literature
span.term: narrative review of the current experimental and correlational literature
span.quote: We review the current research and find that it answers the first of these questions more thoroughly than the second.

span.label: because the theory posits that conspirators use stealth and disinformation, any evidence against it can be read as part of the cover-up - including the debunker
span.quote: Albeit to varying degrees, they are speculative in that they posit actions that are hidden from public scrutiny, complex in that they postulate the coordination of multiple actors, and resistant to falsification in that they postulate that conspirators use stealth and disinformation to cover up their actions—implying that people who try to debunk conspiracy theories may, themselves, be part of the conspiracy.

span.label: disconfirming evidence is recast as the product of a conspiracy, so a cherished belief survives contact with the evidence against it
span.quote: A related property of conspiracy theories is that they can protect cherished beliefs (e.g., vaccination is harmful; climate change is not a serious concern) by casting overwhelmingly disconfirmatory evidence (e.g., scientific findings) as the product of a conspiracy.

span.label: attributing negative outcomes to powerful others lets the self and in-group stay competent and moral while explaining their disadvantage
span.quote: Scholars have suggested that conspiracy theories valorize the self and the in-group by allowing blame for negative outcomes to be attributed to others. Thus, they may help to uphold the image of the self and the in-group as competent and moral but as sabotaged by powerful and unscrupulous others.

span.label: the literature answers what drives conspiracy belief far more thoroughly than what it does to the believer
span.quote: We review the current research and find that it answers the first of these questions more thoroughly than the second.

span.label: the experimental samples are undergraduates and survey panellists who are neither threatened nor inclined to endorse conspiracy theories - not the population the claim is about
span.quote: The experimental research conducted thus far has sampled from populations (undergraduate students and survey panelists) that are not particularly disadvantaged or threatened and that generally do not endorse conspiracy theories. For these people, conspiracy theories are likely to be experienced as unsettling, destabilizing, and potentially alienating. However, these people are not whom scholars have had in mind when they have argued that conspiracy theories may sometimes be adaptive.

span.label: conspiracy theories sometimes turn out to be true, and have brought real elite misconduct to light
span.quote: Furthermore, history has repeatedly shown that corporate and political elites do conspire against public interests. Conspiracy theories play an important role in bringing their misdeeds into the light.

span.label: fair tests require controlled longitudinal work on disadvantaged and threatened populations, which has not been done
span.quote: To conduct fair tests of the utility of conspiracy belief, controlled longitudinal and experimental investigations of disadvantaged and threatened populations are needed. In particular, future research needs to examine individuals whose psychological needs are chronically or experimentally threatened and determine whether conspiracy belief moves them closer to or further away from the fulfillment of these needs.

span.label: the epistemic / existential / social motive taxonomy, carried from system-justification theory into the study of conspiracy belief
span.quote: This research suggests that people may be drawn to conspiracy theories when—compared with nonconspiracy explanations—they promise to satisfy important social psychological motives that can be characterized as epistemic (e.g., the desire for understanding, accuracy, and subjective certainty), existential (e.g., the desire for control and security), and social (e.g., the desire to maintain a positive image of the self or group). This taxonomy, derived from system-justification theory, serves as a useful heuristic to classify the motives associated with conspiracy belief.

span.label: normative standards of causal explanation from the philosophy of science, used to characterise what conspiracy theories are
span.quote: In general, empirically warranted (vs. speculative), parsimonious (vs. complex), and falsifiable explanations are stronger according to normative standards of causal explanation (e.g., in science; see). However, conspiracy theories appear to provide broad, internally consistent explanations that allow people to preserve beliefs in the face of uncertainty and contradiction.

span.label: evidence from the population the claim is about - people whose psychological needs are chronically or experimentally threatened
span.note: eliminates: rival readings of the needs-to-conspiracy link - and the paper's point is that the existing samples CANNOT eliminate them, because the people studied are not the threatened population the claim is about · outcome: absent-stated-about-other
span.quote: The experimental research conducted thus far has sampled from populations (undergraduate students and survey panelists) that are not particularly disadvantaged or threatened and that generally do not endorse conspiracy theories. For these people, conspiracy theories are likely to be experienced as unsettling, destabilizing, and potentially alienating. However, these people are not whom scholars have had in mind when they have argued that conspiracy theories may sometimes be adaptive.

span.label: an experimental baseline for the control manipulation, against which conspiracy belief was compared
span.note: eliminates: a level of conspiracy belief being read as heightened when nothing establishes what the ordinary level is · outcome: held
span.quote: Experiments have shown that compared with baseline conditions, conspiracy belief is heightened when people feel unable to control outcomes and is reduced when their sense of control is affirmed.

span.label: whether exposure to conspiracy theories helps rather than harms - tested directly rather than assumed from the correlational pattern
span.note: eliminates: a correlation between powerlessness and conspiracy belief being read as conspiracy theories SERVING the need - the experiment tests the direction the correlation cannot · outcome: failed
span.quote: On the contrary, experimental exposure to conspiracy theories appears to immediately suppress people’s sense of autonomy and control. These same studies have also shown that it makes people less inclined to take actions that, in the long run, might boost their autonomy and control. Specifically, they are less inclined to commit to their organizations and to engage in mainstream political processes such as voting and party politics.

span.label: whether the trust effect is specific to the institutions a given theory names
span.note: eliminates: a fall in institutional trust that is about the institution the theory names rather than about institutions · outcome: held
span.quote: Experiments show that exposure to conspiracy theories decreases trust in governmental institutions, even if the conspiracy theories are unrelated to those institutions. It also causes disenchantment with politicians and scientists. So far, therefore, empirical research suggests that conspiracy theories serve to erode social capital and may, if anything, frustrate people’s need to see themselves as valuable members of morally decent collectives.

span.label: cheater detection
span.quote: Conspiracy theories may promise to make people feel safer as a form of cheater detection, in which dangerous and untrustworthy individuals are recognized and the threat they posed is reduced or neutralized.

span.label: collective narcissism
span.quote: In keeping with this defensive motivation, conspiracy belief is associated with narcissism—an inflated view of oneself that requires external validation and is linked to paranoid ideation. Conspiracy belief is also predicted by collective narcissism—a belief in the in-group’s greatness paired with a belief that other people do not appreciate it enough.

span.label: anomie
span.quote: A feature of conspiracy theories is their negative, distrustful representation of other people and groups. Thus, it is plausible that they are not only a symptom but also a cause of the feelings of alienation and anomie—a feeling of personal unrest and lack of understanding of the social world—with which they are correlated (e.g.,).

span.label: conspiracy belief is driven by epistemic, existential and social motives, and the evidence does not show it satisfies any of them
span.quote: We conclude that conspiracy belief appears to stem to a large extent from epistemic, existential, and social motives. Research has yet to demonstrate that it effectively serves those motivations, and early indications are that it may often thwart them. It is possible, therefore, that conspiracy belief is a self-defeating form of motivated social cognition.

These same studies have also shown that it makes people less inclined to take actions that, in the long run, might boost their autonomy and control. Specifically, they are less inclined to commit to their organizations and to engage in mainstream political processes such as voting and party politics.
